notes: Real coalition partner is the Country Party, placed in slot 14 as MD does with the Nationals; slot 2 holds the Australia Party (liberal reformers). DLP in 18 (Catholic labourism outside the two blocs of Australian politics). Pro-Moscow CPA minority (later SPA) as slot 6 hardliners. CPA (M-L) Maoists in 19. Icons only where MD sprite shows the same org (Liberals, ALP, CPA, Hizb ut-Tahrir, Country/National Party).

0.name: Australian Security Intelligence Organisation
0.text:
The Australian Security Intelligence Organisation was created in 1949 to counter Soviet espionage and has been led since 1950 by Brigadier Sir Charles Spry. Its officers watch the Communist Party, the anti-war movement, trade unions and foreign diplomats, working closely with MI5 and the CIA.

ASIO sees itself as the shield of the Commonwealth against subversion, and its files reach deep into universities, churches and the Labor movement. It answers to the Attorney-General and has no voters, but in a crisis its intelligence and the trust of conservative ministers would make it a decisive voice.

1.name: Liberal Party of Australia
1.text:
The Liberal Party of Australia, founded by Robert Menzies in 1944, has governed in coalition with the Country Party since 1949. Prime Minister John Gorton, a former RAAF fighter pilot, narrowly survived the October 1969 election, after which William McMahon and David Fairbairn challenged him for the leadership.

The Liberals stand for free enterprise, the American alliance and the forward defence of Australia, with troops still fighting in Vietnam. Gorton's centralism, economic nationalism and impulsive style divide the party room and the state branches. Its base is the business community, the professional middle class and the suburbs of Sydney and Melbourne.

2.name: Australia Party
2.text:
The Australia Party grew out of the Liberal Reform Group formed in 1966 by Liberal voters opposed to conscription for Vietnam, and took its present name in 1969. Its driving force is the Sydney businessman Gordon Barton, owner of IPEC transport, and it contested the 1969 election.

It is a progressive liberal party: against conscription and the Vietnam War, for civil liberties, Aboriginal rights, environmental protection and an independent foreign policy. Its voters are educated, urban and disillusioned with both major parties, and its leverage lies in Senate preferences and in ideas the larger parties are tempted to borrow.

3.name: Australian Labor Party
3.text:
The Australian Labor Party, the oldest party in the country, has been in opposition since 1949 but came within a few seats of victory in October 1969. Gough Whitlam, leader since 1967, has modernised its platform, while the federal executive and the Victorian left still contest his authority.

Labor promises to end conscription and withdraw from Vietnam, recognise the People's Republic of China, fund schools and hospitals, create universal health insurance and grant Aboriginal land rights. Its base is the trade unions and the industrial suburbs, and under Whitlam it is reaching the new educated middle class.

4.name: Communist Party of Australia
4.text:
The Communist Party of Australia, founded in 1920, is legal and holds no seats, but retains a foothold in the trade unions. National Secretary Laurie Aarons leads a reforming majority that condemned the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968 and seeks a broad coalition of the left.

The party opposes the Vietnam War, conscription and the American bases, and demands nationalisation of monopolies and Aboriginal land rights. Its weekly Tribune and its union officials in the metal, building and waterfront industries give it influence beyond its few thousand members, while a pro-Moscow minority fights the leadership.

5.name: Resistance
5.text:
Resistance is a radical youth organisation founded in Sydney in 1967 by students around John and Jim Percy, drawn to the Trotskyist Fourth International. It grew out of Bob Gould's Third World Bookshop milieu and organises against conscription and the Vietnam War.

It calls for immediate withdrawal from Vietnam, draft resistance, solidarity with the National Liberation Front and a socialist Australia built by workers and students. It despises both the Labor right and the Moscow line. Its leverage lies on the campuses and in the streets, where the coming Moratorium campaign promises mass mobilisation.

6.name: The Old Guard
6.text:
The Old Guard is the pro-Soviet minority of the Communist Party of Australia, gathered around the building unionist Pat Clancy, the veteran Edgar Ross and Peter Symon. They opposed the party's condemnation of the invasion of Czechoslovakia and resist Laurie Aarons at every congress.

They defend the leading role of the Soviet Union, democratic centralism and orthodox Marxism-Leninism against the revisionism of the reformers and the New Left. Their strength lies in the Building Workers' Industrial Union and among older militants, and they keep close contact with the Soviet embassy and with Moscow.

7.name: Australia–USSR Friendship Society
7.text:
The Australia–USSR Friendship Society promotes cultural and trade links with the Soviet Union through film evenings, tours, Russian classes and exchanges. Its organisers include communists, Labor left-wingers and Russian-speaking immigrants, and it works hand in hand with the Soviet embassy in Canberra.

It presents the USSR as a peaceful, modern state and campaigns against the American alliance, the bases at Pine Gap and North West Cape, and the Vietnam War. Its membership is small and closely watched by ASIO, but it offers Moscow a respectable channel into Australian unions, universities and cultural life.

8.name: Jam'iyyat Ahl al-Bayt
8.text:
Jam'iyyat Ahl al-Bayt is a circle of Lebanese Shia families in Sydney's inner west who meet in homes and borrowed halls to mark Ashura and teach their children. Most arrived from the south of Lebanon in the last decade and look to the reforming cleric Musa al-Sadr in Tyre.

It seeks a first Shia prayer house, Arabic schooling and recognition alongside the Sunni and Turkish communities. Its outlook is moderate and loyal to Australia, though sympathetic to Palestinian and Lebanese grievances. Its weight lies in extended families, small shops and links to relatives in Lebanon and West Africa.

9.name: Talabat al-Hawza
9.text:
Talabat al-Hawza is a handful of Iranian and Iraqi Shia students at the universities of Sydney and Melbourne who copy and pass around the sermons of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, exiled in Najaf since 1965. They meet discreetly, aware that the Shah's agents watch Iranian students abroad.

They denounce the Pahlavi monarchy, the Iraqi Ba'athists and Western domination, and argue that only rule by the Islamic jurists can bring justice. They have no public presence in Australia, but they are disciplined, mobile and connected to student networks in Europe and the Gulf.

10.name: Australian Federation of Islamic Societies
10.text:
The Australian Federation of Islamic Societies was formed in 1964 to unite the scattered Muslim societies of the country, from Adelaide's Afghan cameleer heritage to the new Turkish, Lebanese, Albanian and Cypriot communities. It coordinates mosque projects and religious instruction.

Its leadership is conservative, respectable and loyal to the Commonwealth, preferring quiet dealings with governments to politics. It welcomes help from the Muslim World League and Saudi Arabia, whose scholarships and funds shape its religious line, and its leverage lies in being the recognised voice of Australian Muslims before the authorities.

11.name: Hizb ut-Tahrir
11.text:
Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Islamic Liberation Party founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by Taqiuddin al-Nabhani, has a few adherents among Arab students and young migrants in Sydney and Melbourne. They receive pamphlets from Beirut and meet in small, closed study circles.

The party rejects nationalism, democracy and both superpowers, and calls for a restored caliphate ruling all Muslims by Islamic law. It renounces violence by its members but hopes to win over army officers in Muslim lands. In Australia it is negligible in numbers, yet it attracts young men angered by the 1967 war.

12.name: Usrah Kampus
12.text:
Usrah Kampus is a network of small study 'families' formed by Malaysian and Indonesian Colombo Plan students at Australian universities. Modelled on the Muslim Brotherhood's usrah system, the circles meet weekly to study the Qur'an and the writings of Hasan al-Banna and Abul A'la Mawdudi.

They aim to form a disciplined Islamic elite that will return home to reform society by preaching rather than revolution, and they are hostile to both communism and Western secularism. Their influence in Australia is small, but they shape future engineers, doctors and civil servants of Southeast Asia.

13.name: Department of the Treasury
13.text:
The Commonwealth Treasury is the most powerful department in Canberra, headed by Secretary Sir Richard Randall. Its economists control the budget, the loans to the states and economic advice to cabinet, and they clash with Gorton's interventionist instincts and with John McEwen's Department of Trade and Industry.

The Treasury stands for sound finance, low inflation, lower tariffs and the authority of officials over politicians. Its leverage lies in the budget process, its ties to the Reserve Bank and a network of mandarins who expect to outlast any government.

14.name: Australian Country Party
14.text:
The Australian Country Party is the junior partner of the Coalition and holds the Deputy Prime Ministership through John McEwen, its leader since 1958 and Minister for Trade and Industry. Doug Anthony is his likely successor.

It speaks for wheat, wool, sugar and dairy farmers and for country towns, demanding stable prices, subsidies and rural infrastructure. McEwen's policy of 'protection all round' combines tariffs for industry with marketing boards for farmers, and the party's leverage over the Liberals far exceeds its share of the vote.

15.name: Broken Hill Proprietary Company
15.text:
The Broken Hill Proprietary Company is Australia's largest enterprise, controlling the steelworks at Newcastle, Port Kembla and Whyalla, iron ore interests and, with Esso, the new Bass Strait oil and gas fields. Its managing director Sir Ian McLennan stands at the centre of the Melbourne business establishment.

BHP and the mining houses favour foreign capital, low company taxes and freedom from Canberra's controls, though they welcome protection for steel. They fund the Liberal Party, sit on the boards of the banks and press for the development of the north. Their leverage is sheer economic weight.

16.name: Institute of Public Affairs
16.text:
The Institute of Public Affairs was founded in Melbourne in 1943 by businessmen to defend free enterprise against Labor's post-war planning. Its director C. D. Kemp edits the IPA Review and supplies arguments to Liberal politicians and business leaders.

It calls for lower taxes, smaller government, competition and the curbing of union power, and it is uneasy about high tariffs and Gorton's economic nationalism. It has no members in Parliament, but its publications, lectures and the companies that fund it give it a steady voice in Melbourne boardrooms and the press.

17.name: Australian Conservation Foundation
17.text:
The Australian Conservation Foundation was established in 1965 with Commonwealth support to promote the protection of nature. Its president is Sir Garfield Barwick, Chief Justice of the High Court, and its council includes scientists, graziers and businessmen.

It pushes for national parks, the protection of the Great Barrier Reef from oil drilling and limestone mining, and the scientific management of land and wildlife. Cautious and establishment-minded, it relies on lobbying rather than protest, but younger members want a more combative stance as the campaigns over Lake Pedder and the Reef grow.

18.name: Democratic Labor Party
18.text:
The Democratic Labor Party was born from the Labor split of 1955, when anti-communist Catholics broke away from the ALP. Led by Senator Vince Gair and guided from outside by B. A. Santamaria's National Civic Council, it holds the balance of power in the Senate.

It combines labourist economics, family allowances and state aid to Catholic schools with fierce anti-communism and support for the war in Vietnam. Its preferences keep Labor out of office, and its leverage lies in Senate votes, Catholic working-class voters in Melbourne and the unions it still controls.

19.name: Communist Party of Australia (Marxist–Leninist)
19.text:
The Communist Party of Australia (Marxist–Leninist) was founded in 1964 by the Melbourne barrister Ted Hill, who split from the CPA in support of Beijing. It is small and secretive but publishes the weekly Vanguard and has influence in some Victorian unions and on the Monash campus.

It follows Mao Zedong Thought, denounces Soviet social-imperialism as fiercely as American imperialism, and calls for revolution and genuine national independence. Its leverage lies in its militant students, its hold on the Builders Labourers in Victoria and its links to Beijing.

20.name: Australian League of Rights
20.text:
The Australian League of Rights was founded in 1946 by Eric Butler, a Social Credit publicist from Melbourne. It works through newsletters, 'actionist' study groups and infiltration of country branches of the Liberal and Country parties.

It campaigns against communism, the United Nations, international bankers and Asian immigration, defends Rhodesia and the Crown, and spreads antisemitic conspiracy theories. Its support lies in rural Victoria, Queensland and Western Australia among farmers squeezed by falling wool prices, and its leverage comes from discipline rather than numbers.

21.name: National Socialist Party of Australia
21.text:
The National Socialist Party of Australia is a small neo-Nazi group active in Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane, formed by militants of the earlier Australian National Socialist Party. Its members wear uniforms, hold provocative rallies and distribute propaganda from American and British neo-Nazis.

It preaches white supremacy, the White Australia policy in its harshest form, antisemitism and violent anti-communism. It has no electoral weight and is closely watched by the police and ASIO, but its street activism and links to the international neo-Nazi scene give it a capacity for provocation.

22.name: Australian Army
22.text:
The Australian Army has fought in South Vietnam since 1962 and keeps the 1st Australian Task Force at Nui Dat in Phuoc Tuy Province, filled partly by national servicemen. Lieutenant General Sir Thomas Daly is Chief of the General Staff, under General Sir John Wilton as Chairman of the Chiefs of Staff Committee.

The officer corps is professional, apolitical and committed to forward defence and the American alliance, and worries about the strain of conscription and the anti-war movement on morale. It has no tradition of intervening in politics, but in an emergency its prestige and the Coalition's trust would carry great weight.

23.name: House of Windsor
23.text:
Elizabeth II reigns as Queen of Australia, represented by Governor-General Sir Paul Hasluck, the former Minister for External Affairs who took office in 1969. The Crown stands at the apex of the Commonwealth and state constitutions, and the Queen is expected to tour Australia this year for the Cook bicentenary.

Monarchists defend the Crown as the guarantor of parliamentary government, British heritage and continuity, and oppose the faint republican stirrings among intellectuals and Labor radicals. Their strength lies in the RSL, the Liberal and Country parties, the armed forces and older Anglo-Australian voters.
